Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 39, verse 1:

(p-240) (Sūrat al-Zumar is Meccan, except His saying: ﴿O My servants...﴾ to the end of the verse. Its verses are seventy-five.)

﴿The revelation of the Book﴾ is a predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada'), which is a demonstrative pronoun (ism ishara) by which the surah is indicated, treating it as if it were present and pointed to, because it is in a position of exalted mention and presence, as has passed many times. It has been said: it is a pronoun referring back to the "Reminder" in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is only a reminder to the worlds﴾ (38:87). And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿from Allah, the Mighty, the Wise﴾ is a complement (silah) of "the revelation," or a second predicate, or a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of "the revelation," its operative being the sense of the demonstrative, or of "the Book," which is the object of the sense of its operative (the verbal noun) that is annexed. It has also been said: it is a predicate of "the revelation of the Book." The first view is the correct one. Or it is according to what the context requires, which is the explanation that the surah, or the Qur'an, is the revelation of the Book from Allah exalted is He, not an explanation that the revelation of the Book is from Him exalted is He and not from anyone else, as the last view indicates. It has been recited as (tanzīla) al-Kitāb with the accusative, by supposing a verb such as "recite" (iqra') or "adhere to" (ilzam). The mention of the two attributes, might (ʿizza) and wisdom (ḥikma), serves to announce the manifestation of their effects in the Book through the operation of its rulings and the enforcement of its commands and prohibitions without any opposer or preventer, and through the foundation of all that is in it upon the basis of brilliant wisdoms. And His saying, exalted is He:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 39, verse 2:

﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you the Book in truth﴾. This begins an explanation of the status of that which was sent down to him (ﷺ), and of what is incumbent upon him following the explanation of the status of what was sent down and of its being from Allah the Exalted. The intended meaning of "the Book" (al-Kitab) is the Qur'an, and its being stated explicitly, on the assumption that it is what is meant by the first mention too, serves to glorify it and to show greater concern for its matter. The "ba'" (bi) in "bil-haqq" (in truth) is either connected to "the sending down," meaning: by means of the truth, its establishment, and its manifestation; or it is connected to the motive of the truth and its requirement for the sending down. Or it is connected to something omitted which is a circumstantial clause (hal) either from the "nun" of majesty (the royal "We") or from "the Book," meaning: We sent it down to you while being upright in that matter; or We sent it down to you accompanied by truth and rightness, meaning: everything in it is truth, without doubt, requiring acting upon it as a binding obligation.

The "fa'" (fa) in the words of the Exalted, ﴿So worship Allah, making the religion sincerely His﴾, is for the consequence of the command to worship upon the sending down of the Book to him, peace and blessings be upon him, with the truth. That is: worship Him, the Exalted, dedicating the religion to Him purely, free from the admixtures of polytheism and showing off, as has been clarified in the midst of what has been sent down to you. It has also been read with the "al-din" (the religion) in the nominative case, as the subject (mubtada') whose predicate is the preceding adverbial phrase, to emphasise the exclusivity derived from the "lam" (of exclusivity); and the sentence is a resumptive clause that serves as a justification for the command to sincere worship. The words of the Exalted:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 39, verse 3:

﴿Surely, to God belongs the pure religion.﴾ (p-241) It is a resumptive clause (isti'naf muqarrir) confirming what precedes it of the command to make religion sincerely devoted to Him, exalted is He, and the obligation of complying with it. According to the last reading, it is an emphatic clause (mu'akkid) affirming the exclusivity of religion to Him, exalted is He; that is: "Surely, it is He who must be singled out for sincere obedience to Him, because He alone possesses the attributes of divinity (sifat al-uluhiyyah), among whose components is knowledge of the innermost secrets and hearts." His exalted saying: ﴿And those who take protectors besides Him﴾ is a verification of the truth of what was mentioned of sincerity of religion (ikhlas al-din), which is an expression for monotheism (tawhid), by demonstrating the falsity of polytheism (shirk), which is an expression for abandoning its sincerity. The relative pronoun (al-mawsul) is an expression for the polytheists, and its position is nominative (raf') by way of inception (ibtida'), its predicate (khabar) being the clause introduced by "inna" that will come later. "The protectors" refers to the angels, Jesus, peace be upon them, and the idols. His exalted saying: ﴿We only worship them so that they may bring us near to God in closeness﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) with an implied "saying" (taqdir al-qawl), from the waw of "they took," explaining the manner of their polytheism and the non-sincerity of their religion. The exception (istithna') is an exception from the most general of causes (mufarragh min a'amm al-'ilal). "Zulfa" is a verbal noun (masdar) emphasizing a verb of a different root that shares its meaning, that is: "And those who did not sincerely devote worship to God, exalted is He, but mixed it with the worship of others, saying: 'We do not worship them for anything whatsoever except that they bring us near to God, exalted is He, as a bringing near.'"

﴿Surely God will judge between them﴾: that is, between them and their opponents, who are the sincere adherents of the religion. It has been elided because the context indicates it, as in His exalted saying: ﴿We do not make any distinction between any of His messengers﴾ according to one of the two interpretations; that is: between one of them and another. On this basis is the saying of al-Nabigha:

"There was not between al-Khayr, even had he come safe, and Abu Hujr, except a few nights."

That is: between al-Khayr and me. It has also been said that the pronoun in "between them" refers to both groups together.

﴿concerning that about which they differ﴾: concerning the religion about which they differ, in monotheism and polytheism, and each group claims the correctness of what it adopts. His judgment in this matter is the admission of the monotheists into Paradise and the polytheists into the Fire. Thus the pronoun refers to both groups; this is what the course of the noble composition requires. As for the permissibility that the relative pronoun refers to the worshipped ones, with the returning pronoun elided and the polytheists implied without mention, relying on the indication of the context, the sense being: "And those whom the polytheists took as protectors, saying, 'We do not worship them except that they bring us near to God. Surely God will judge between them,' that is, between the worshippers and the worshipped, concerning that about which they differ, since the worshippers hope for their intercession while they curse them" — then, after overlooking what it contains of forced interpretations, it is far from soundness. How could it be otherwise, since in what has been mentioned of seeking intercession and cursing there is no matter over which the two groups differ in a way that requires judgment and decision? Rather, that refers to the difference between the groups of monotheists and polytheists in this world concerning the religion, which persists until the Day of Resurrection. It has been read: ("They say: We do not worship them"), so it is a substitute (badal) for the relative clause, not a predicate of the relative pronoun, as has been said, since there is no added excellence in reporting it. It has also been read: ("We do not worship you except that you bring us near") as a quotation of what they addressed to their gods, and it has been read: ("We worship them") with the vowel of the "ba'" being assimilated.

﴿Surely God does not guide﴾: that is, He does not grant success in guidance to the truth, which is the path of salvation from what is disliked and the attainment of what is sought.

﴿him who is a liar, an ingrate﴾: that is, firmly established in lying, excessive in disbelief, as is expressed by the reading "kadhdhab" and "kadhub," for these two lack insight and are not receptive to guidance, because they have altered the original natural disposition through habituation in error and persistence in deviation. The sentence is a justification for what was mentioned of His judgment.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 39, verse 4:

﴿Had God desired to take a son...﴾ . . . etc. It is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) driven toward establishing the truth and refuting the claim that the angels are God's daughters and that 'Isa is His son, exalted is He far above that with a great exaltation, by demonstrating the impossibility of taking a son with respect to Him, may He be exalted, in an absolute sense, so that the impossibility of what precedes is included in it by primary inclusion (p-242), namely: Had God desired to take a son.

﴿He would have chosen﴾ i.e., He would have taken.

﴿from among what He creates﴾ i.e., from among the totality of what He creates, or from the kind of what He creates.

﴿whatever He wills﴾ to take it. For there is no existent other than Him except that it is a creature of His, Exalted is He, due to the impossibility of plurality of the Necessary Existent (wajib al-wujud), and the necessity that all else be traced back to Him. It is evident that taking a son is contingent upon similarity between the one who takes and the one who is taken, and that a creature does not resemble its Creator such that it could be taken as a son. Therefore, what we supposed to be the taking of a son is not the taking of a son but rather the choosing of a servant, and to this I point. Here choosing (istifa') is placed in the position of taking (ittikhadh), which the conditional structure requires, as a warning about the impossibility of its antecedent, because supposing its occurrence, indeed supposing the will for its occurrence, entails its non-existence. That is: Had God, Exalted is He, desired to take a son, He would have done something that is not taking a son at all, but is only the choosing of a servant. There is no doubt that what entails, upon supposing its occurrence, its non-existence is certainly impossible. So it is as if it were said: Had God desired to take a son, it would have been impossible and would not have been valid. But not on the basis that the impossibility is contingent upon the realization of the will, rather on the basis that it is realized in its absence by way of greater priority, along the lines of: "Had he not feared God, he would not have disobeyed Him."

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Glory be to Him﴾, is a confirmation of what was mentioned regarding the impossibility of taking a son with respect to Him, Exalted is He, and an affirmation of it by explaining His transcendence above it. That is: He is transcendent in His essence above that with a transcendence specific to Him. It is also said that "subhan" is a verbal noun from "sabaha" meaning "to be far away," or from "asbaha" meaning to glorify Him with a fitting glorification, or that it is a proper name for glorification said upon the tongues of servants, or that they glorified Him with a glorification befitting His station.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿He is God, the One, the Subduer﴾ is a resumptive clause explaining His transcendence in terms of attributes, following the explanation of His transcendence above it in terms of essence. The attribute of divinity (uluhiyya), which entails all attributes of perfection and negates marks of deficiency, together with the essential unity (wahda dhatiyya) that necessitates the impossibility of similarity and sharing between Him, Exalted is He, and anything else in an absolute sense, decrees, with perfected decree, His transcendence above what they say. Likewise the attribute of subjugation (qahhariyya), since taking a son is the affair of one who is under the dominion of another, subject to annihilation, so that his son may stand in his place upon his passing, whereas He who is impossible to annihilate is the subduer of all beings. How could it be conceived that He would take, from among perishable things, something to stand in His place?

His saying, Exalted is He:

﴿He created the heavens and the earth with truth﴾ is an elaboration of some of His acts, exalted is He, which indicate His singularity with respect to the sublime attributes mentioned. That is: He created them and what is between them of existing things, conjoined with truth and rightness, comprising wisdoms and benefits. And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He wraps the night over the day and wraps the day over the night﴾ is an explanation of the manner of His disposal of them after explaining their creation, for the occurrence of night and day on earth is contingent upon the movement of the heavens. That is, each of them covers the other, as if He wraps it around it like the wrapping of clothing around the one who wears it, or conceals it with it as the wrapped thing is concealed by the wrapping, or makes it turn around it in successive turning, like the successive winding of a turban. The form of the present tense indicates renewal.

﴿And He subjected the sun and the moon﴾ made them submissive to His command, exalted is He. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿each runs for an appointed term﴾ is an explanation of the manner of their subjection. That is, each of them runs until the end of its cycle or the cessation of its motion, and its detail has been explained more than once.

﴿Verily, He is the Mighty﴾, the Victorious, the Able over every thing, among which is the punishment of the disobedient.

﴿the Forgiving﴾, the one who is exceedingly forgiving. Therefore He does not hasten punishment and deprive [them] of what is in these wondrous creations of the traces of mercy. The opening of the sentence with the particle of alerting is to show complete attentiveness to its content. (p-243)

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 39, verse 6:

﴿He created you from a single soul﴾ is an elucidation of another of His acts that point to what has been mentioned. The omission of its coordination with the creation of the heavens serves to signal that it is independent in indicating [the Creator's power], and because it is connected to the lower world. It begins with the creation of man because of its antiquity as a sign, owing to what it contains of marvelous effects of power and secrets of wisdom, and its primacy in knowledge, for a man knows his own state best. By "soul" (nafs) is meant the soul of Adam, peace be upon him. His saying: ﴿then He made from it its mate﴾ is a conjunction with something omitted that is an attribute of "soul," i.e., from a soul He created, then made from it its mate. Or it is conjoined to the sense of "single," i.e., from a soul that was made one, then He made from it its mate and so made them a pair. Or it is conjoined to "He created you," owing to the difference between the two in indicating [the Creator's power]: although both are signs indicating what has been mentioned, the first, because it has continued, has become customary, whereas the second, since it was not customary and lies outside the measure of the first, as the expression of it by "making" rather than "creating" suggests, is more fitting to be a sign and more apt to cause the hearer to marvel. Therefore it is conjoined to the first with "then," indicating its distinction from it in excellence and merit, and its remoteness from it in what pertains to the increase of its being a sign; this is remoteness in state and rank. It has been said: He brought forth the offspring of Adam from his loins like specks, then created Hawwa' (Eve) from him. In this there are three signs in sequence: the creation of Adam, peace be upon him, without father or mother; the creation of Hawwa' from his rib (qusayra); then the dispersal of the creation from the two of them, which is the reason for the restriction. His exalted saying: ﴿and He sent down for you﴾ is an elucidation of another of His acts that point to what has been mentioned, i.e., He decreed, or apportioned, for you. For His decrees and His apportionment are described as descending from heaven, since they are recorded in the Preserved Tablet; or He brought into being for you, by means of causes descending from heaven, such as rains and the rays of the stars.

﴿of the cattle eight pairs﴾ male and female: they are the camel, the cow, the sheep and the goat. It has been said: He created them in Paradise and then sent them down. The fronting of the two adverbial phrases before the direct object is, as has been noted many times, for the sake of giving attention to what was fronted and arousing eagerness for what was delayed, for the fact that the sending down is for their benefits, and that it is from the high direction, are among the important matters that make one eager for what is sent down inevitably. His exalted saying: ﴿He creates you in the wombs of your mothers﴾ is a resumptive sentence set forth to explain the manner of their creation and its various stages, which indicate overwhelming power. The use of the present tense indicates gradualness and renewal. His exalted saying: ﴿creation after creation﴾ is an emphatic verbal noun, i.e., He creates you therein a creation that comes after a creation, i.e., a creation proceeding gradually, a sound living being, after bones clothed with flesh, after bare bones, after lumps (mudgha) formed, after lumps not formed, after a clot ('alaqa), after a drop (nutfa).

﴿in three darknesses﴾ is connected to ﴿He creates you﴾. They are the darkness of the belly, the darkness of the womb, and the darkness of the placenta (mashima); or the darkness of the spine (sulb), the belly, and the womb.

﴿That is﴾ is a reference to Him, exalted is He, in view of the acts mentioned; and the sense of distance in it signals the remoteness of His station in greatness and majesty. Its place is nominative as the subject: That is the One of mighty affair whose acts I have enumerated.

﴿Allah﴾ and His exalted saying: ﴿your Lord﴾ is another predicate, i.e., the Nurturer of you in what has been mentioned of the stages and in what follows them, and your Owner, the One deserving that worship be restricted to Him.

﴿To Him belongs the dominion﴾ absolutely, in this world and the next; no other has any share in that in any respect. The sentence is another predicate, and likewise His exalted saying: ﴿there is no god but He﴾. The "fa" in His exalted saying: ﴿how then are you turned away?﴾ is for the sequencing of what follows upon the matters of His exalted state that have been mentioned, i.e., how then are you turned away from worshipping Him, exalted is He, despite the abundance of the reasons and motives for it and the complete absence of any impediment to it, toward worshipping other than Him, without any motive for it, despite the multitude of deterrents from it?!

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 39, verse 7:

﴿If you disbelieve﴾ in Him, exalted is He, after witnessing the various kinds of His blessings that have been mentioned, and knowing His great affairs, which necessitate faith and gratitude.

﴿then indeed Allah is Free of need from you﴾. That is: know that He, exalted is He, is free of need from your faith and your gratitude, and is not affected by their absence.

﴿And He does not approve of disbelief for His servants﴾. That is: His not being pleased with the disbelief of His servants is for their benefit and to repel harm from them, out of mercy toward them, not because He would be harmed by it, exalted is He.

﴿And if you are grateful, He approves it for you﴾. That is: He approves gratitude for your sake and your benefit, since it is a means for you to attain the happiness of both abodes, not because He benefits from it, exalted is He. It was said "for His servants" rather than "for you" in order to generalize the ruling and to give its reason as their being His servants, exalted is He. It was also read with the ha' (ه) pronounced with a sukun (ـْ), i.e., "yarḍhu" (يَرْضَهْ).

﴿And no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾. This is a statement that the disbelief of the disbeliever does not spread to anyone else at all. That is: no soul carrying a burden bears the burden of another soul.

﴿Then to your Lord is your return﴾ through resurrection after death.

﴿Then He will inform you﴾ at that time ﴿of what you used to do﴾. That is: what you used to do in the world of deeds of disbelief and faith; that is, He will recompense you for that with reward and punishment.

﴿Indeed, He is Knowing of what is within the breasts﴾. That is: of what the hearts conceal, so how much more so of the outward deeds! This is a reason given for the informing.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 39, verse 8:

﴿When harm touches man﴾ from sickness or other things, ﴿he calls upon his Lord, turning back to Him in repentance﴾, returning to Him from what he used to call upon in times of ease, knowing that he is far beyond the power to remove his harm. This is a description of the species through the condition of some of its individuals, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, man is ever a wrongdoer, ungrateful﴾.

﴿Then when He bestows upon him a favor from Himself﴾, that is, He gives him a great blessing from His presence, exalted is He, from al-takhawwul (takhawwul), which means al-ta'ahhud (care, attentiveness). That is, He makes him a khail (caretaker) of wealth, from their saying: "So-and-so is a khail of wealth" when he is attentive to it and good in looking after it. Or it is from al-khawal (khawal), which means boasting; that is, He makes him yakhul, that is, he becomes arrogant and boastful.

﴿He forgets what he used to call upon Him for﴾, that is, he forgets the harm for which he used to call upon God, exalted is He, to remove it earlier.

﴿Before﴾, that is, before the bestowal, or he forgets his Lord whom he used to call upon and humbly beseech, either based on the view that "ma" (what) here means "man" (who), as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And by Him who created the male and the female﴾ and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Nor are you worshippers of what I worship﴾; or to indicate that his forgetting has reached the point where he does not know what he is calling upon, let alone knowing who He is, as has passed in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿of what she suckled﴾.

﴿And he sets up rivals to God﴾, partners in worship, ﴿to lead astray﴾ people by this ﴿from His way﴾, which is monotheism. It has been read: (liyadilla) with a fatha on the ya, that is, he increases in going astray or persists in it. Otherwise, the origin of going astray is not later than the aforementioned setting up. The "lam" is the lam of consequence (lam al-'aqibah), as in His saying, exalted is He: (p-245) ﴿So the family of Pharaoh picked him up, that he might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾, except that this is closer to the reality, because the one who sets up here intends by his mentioned setting up the actual misguiding and going astray, even if he does not recognize, due to his ignorance, that they are misguidance and going astray. As for the family of Pharaoh, they did not intend enmity at all by their picking him up.

﴿Say﴾, as a threat to that misguided misleader, and as a clarification of his condition and his end.

﴿Enjoy your disbelief a little﴾, that is, a little enjoyment, or for a little time.

﴿Indeed, you are of the companions of the Fire﴾, that is, of those who are constantly bound to it and tormented in it forever. This is a reason for the little enjoyment, and in it is a discouragement from salvation that is not hidden, as if it were said: since you have refused to accept what you were commanded of faith and obedience, it is your right to be commanded to abandon it so that you may taste its punishment.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 39, verse 9:**

﴿Is he who is devoutly obedient during the hours of the night . . .﴾ etc. This is part of the speech that was commanded. The particle *"am"* (أم) is either *muttasila* (connected, *ittisal* meaning joined to what precedes it) with its counterpart (*mu'adil*, أمٌ معادِلُها) omitted, relying on the sense of the context to indicate it. It is as if it were said to him, as an emphasis of the threat and a mockery of him: "Are you better in state and in outcome, or is it one who is steadfast in the duties of obedience and persistent in performing the acts of worship during the hours of the night, in both states of ease and hardship, not only at the touch of harm, as is your habit, while being in that condition?" ﴿Prostrating and standing﴾, meaning combining the two praiseworthy descriptions. The mention of prostration before standing is because it is more inclusive of the meaning of worship. Both have been read in the nominative case (*raf'*), as a predicate after a predicate (*khabar ba'da khabar*).

﴿Fearing the Hereafter﴾ is another circumstantial qualifier (*hal*, a clause describing the state of the subject) in succession or overlapping with the previous ones, or it is a resumptive clause (*isti'naf*, a new sentence that begins independently) that comes as an answer to what arises from the description of his state of devotion, prostration and standing. It is as if it were said: "Why does he do that?" And it is answered: "He fears the punishment of the Hereafter."

﴿And hoping for the mercy of his Lord﴾, so he is saved by this from what he fears and attains what he hopes for. This is as indicated by the mention of the title of Lordship (*rububiyya*), which points to the bringing to perfection, together with its attribution to the pronoun of the one who hopes. It is not that he fears only the harm of this world and hopes only for its good.

Or it is disconnected (*munqati'a*), and what it contains of the turning away (*idrab*) is for the transition from the threat to rebuke, by imposing an answer that compels acknowledgment of the clear contrast between the two. It is as if it were said: "Rather, is the one who is devoutly obedient . . . better, or the one who is a disbeliever like you?" This is the meaning also according to the reading with the lightened form (*takhfif*).

﴿Say﴾ as a clarification of the truth and an alert to the nobility of knowledge and action.

﴿Are those who know﴾ the realities of conditions, and so act in accordance with their knowledge, like the devout one mentioned, ﴿equal to those who do not know﴾, meaning what has been mentioned, or anything, and so act in accordance with their ignorance and error, like your habit. The interrogation is to alert to the fact that the former being at the highest ascents of good, and the latter being at the farthest levels of evil, is so evident that it is hardly hidden from anyone, fair or stubborn. It has also been said that this comes by way of comparison, meaning: just as those who know and those who do not know are not equal, the obedient and the disobedient are not equal.

The statement of the Exalted, ﴿Only those of understanding are mindful﴾, is an independent sentence, not included in the speech that was commanded. It comes from Him, the Exalted, after the command to mention the striking admonitions that restrain from disbelief and sins, to show that they have no effect on the hearts of the disbelievers because their minds are disordered. This is as in the verse of the one who said:

*"Halt, and greet the traces of the abode of Nu'ma; what greeting can be given to a ditch and stones?"*

That is: only those whose minds are pure of the flaws of defect take admonition from these clear explanations, and these are far removed from that.

It is also read: (*innama yadhdhakkaru*) with assimilation (*idgham*).

(p-246) "Say: O My servants who have believed, fear your Lord." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was commanded to admonish the believers and to urge them toward taqwa (God-consciousness, fear of God) and obedience, following the specification of the admonition to "those endowed with understanding" (ulu al-albab), as a notice that they are the ones meant, as will be stated explicitly. That is, "Say to them this very word of mine." In it there is an honouring of them by attributing them to the Divine Name (ḍamīr al-jalālah, the pronoun of majesty), and an extra emphasis on the importance of the thing commanded, for conveying the very command of God is more effective in making compliance obligatory. His saying, exalted is He: "For those who do good" (lil-ladhīna aḥsanū) is an explanation of the command, or of the obligation of complying with it. The mention of ihsan (doing good) within the relative clause, rather than taqwa, is to notify that it is of the category of ihsan, and that the two are mutually entailing; likewise patience (ṣabr), as has passed in His saying: "Indeed God is with those who fear Him and those who are doers of good," and in His saying: "Indeed whoever fears and is patient, then indeed God does not waste the reward of the doers of good." His saying: "In this world" (fī hādhihi al-dunyā) is related to aḥsanū, that is, they performed good deeds in this world in the manner of sincerity (ikhlāṣ), which is what the Messenger of God (ﷺ) expressed when he was asked about ihsan, saying (ﷺ): "That you worship God as if you see Him, and if you do not see Him, then indeed He sees you."

"A good" (ḥasanah): that is, a great good, the reality of which cannot be comprehended; and it is Paradise. It has been said that it is related to ḥasanah in the sense of an explanation of its place, or a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from its pronoun in the adverbial phrase; so what is meant by it then is health and well-being (al-ṣiḥḥah wa al-ʿāfiyah).

"And God's earth is spacious": so whoever finds it difficult to devote himself fully to taqwa and ihsan in his homeland, let him emigrate to where he is able to do so, as is the practice of the prophets and the righteous, for he has no excuse at all for negligence. His saying, exalted is He: "Indeed the patient will be given their reward in full..." etc. is an encouragement toward the taqwa that was commanded. The choice of "the patient" over "the God-fearing" is to notify that they possess the virtue of patience just as they possess the virtue of ihsan, in view of what has been indicated concerning the entailment of taqwa for both, along with what it contains of greater urging toward perseverance (muṣābarah) and striving (mujāhadah) in bearing the hardships and toils of emigration. That is: "Indeed those who were patient in their religion, who guarded its limits, and who did not neglect the observance of its rights will be given their reward in full, for what they endured in that of the various kinds of pains and trials, of which the leaving of family and the departure from homelands is among the most."

"Their reward" (ajrahum): in return for what they underwent of patience.

"Without reckoning" (bi-ghayri ḥisāb): that is, in such a way that it is not counted and not confined. From Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with them both: it is not reached by the reckoning of the reckoners, nor is it known. In a hadith it is related that on the Day of Resurrection the scales will be set up for the people of prayer, charity and pilgrimage, and they will be given their rewards by them; but no scales will be set up for the people of trial, rather the reward will be poured upon them in abundance, so much so that the people of well-being in the world will wish that their bodies were being cut with scissors, because of the excellence that the people of trial will carry away.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 39, verse 11:

﴿Say: Indeed, I have been commanded to worship Allah, being sincere to Him in religion.﴾ That is: free from everything that contradicts it, such as shirk (associating partners with Allah) and riya' (showing off), and other things besides these. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was commanded to make clear what he himself had been commanded regarding sincerity (ikhlas) in the worship of Allah, which is an expression of what the believers were commanded regarding taqwa (God-consciousness), by way of emphasis in urging them to carry out what they were obligated to do, and as a preparation for what follows, which is addressed to the polytheists.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 39, verse 12:

﴿And I have been commanded to be the first of the Muslims.﴾ That is: "And I have been commanded in this, so that I may be foremost among them (p-247) in this world and the Hereafter; for attaining the prize of precedence in religion (qasab al-sabq) is through sincerity in it. The conjunction (al-'atf) is used because the second (clause) differs from the first by being restricted by the cause (al-'illa), and it indicates that the aforementioned act of worship, just as it requires the command to perform it for its own sake, also requires it for what follows from it of precedence in religion." It is also permissible to consider the lam (la-) as superfluous (mazida), as in "aradtu li-an aqum" (I wanted to stand), based on the saying of the Exalted: ﴿I have been commanded to be the first of those who submit﴾. So the meaning is: "And I have been commanded to be the first of those who submit among the people of my time, or among my people, or to be the first to call others to what I have called myself to."

﴿Say, "Indeed, I fear, if I disobey my Lord,﴾ by abandoning sincere devotion (ikhlas) and inclining toward the polytheism you are upon,

﴿the punishment of a tremendous day.﴾ That is the Day of Resurrection, described as "tremendous" because of the magnitude of the calamities and terrors that occur in it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 39, verse 14:

﴿Say: It is Allah I worship﴾ — alone, not another besides Him, neither independently nor in association.

﴿sincerely devoted to Him in my religion﴾ — free from every admixture. He ﷺ was first commanded to declare that he is commanded to worship Allah the Exalted and to devote the religion to Him; then he was commanded to inform them of his fear of punishment should he disobey; then he was commanded to inform them of his compliance with the command in the most emphatic and forceful manner, to manifest his steadfastness in the religion, to cut off their vain hopes, and to pave the way for threatening them with the words of the Exalted:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 39, verse 15:

﴿So worship what you will﴾ besides Him, [meaning] other than Him, the Exalted. In this there is a clear indication of the intensity of His anger toward them, as if, when they did not desist from what they had been forbidden, they were commanded to do it so that punishment would befall them.

﴿Say: Indeed, the losers﴾, that is, those who are complete in loss (khusran), which is an expression for the squandering of what matters to a person and the destruction of what is indispensable to him, ﴿are those who have lost themselves and their families﴾ by their choosing disbelief for both of them; that is, they wasted them and destroyed them.

﴿On the Day of Resurrection﴾, when they enter the Fire, where they have exposed themselves and their families to everlasting punishment, and brought them into a ruin beyond which there is no ruin. It has also been said: they lost their families, because if they were among the people of the Fire, they lost them just as they lost themselves, and if they were among the people of Paradise, they have departed from them in a departure with no return after it. In this view there is an objection: what is feared is the loss of that which, were it to return, the loser would benefit from, and that is not conceivable in the last alternative. It has also been said: they lost them, because they did not enter the place of those who would be among the people of Paradise, and they lost their families whom they would have enjoyed had they believed. Whatever the case, the intent is not merely to define the complete losers by what we mention, but to state that they are these people, either by making the relative clause (al-ladhina) an expression for them, or for what they are included in at the first level of inclusion. And what is in His words, ﴿Indeed, that is the manifest loss﴾, is a resumption of the sentence, introduced with the particle of alerting (alā) and the demonstrative (dhalika), indicating the remoteness of the status of the one referred to in evil; the insertion of the pronoun of separation (damir al-fasl), the definiteness of "loss" (al-khusran), and describing it as "manifest" (al-mubin) indicate the perfection of its terror and atrocity, and that there is no loss beyond it, which is not hidden. And His words, exalted is He:

(p-248) ﴿For them there will be canopies of fire above them﴾ ... etc. This is a kind of explanation of their loss, after its terrifying nature has been conveyed in an indefinite manner. "For them" is the predicate (khabar) of "canopies" (zulal), and "from above them" is connected to an omitted element (mutaʿalliq bi-mahdhuf). It has been said that it is a circumstantial clause (hal) modifying "canopies," but the more evident view is that it is a circumstantial clause modifying the pronoun in the preceding adverbial phrase, and "of the Fire" is an attributive modifier (sifah) of "canopies." That is: for them are many canopies, piled one above another, from above them, consisting of Fire.

﴿And from beneath them﴾ likewise ﴿canopies﴾, i.e., many layers, some beneath others, are canopies for others. Rather, for them too, as they plunge down into its levels.

﴿That﴾ dreadful punishment is what ﴿Allah causes His servants to fear﴾, and warns them of it through verses of warning, so that they may avoid what would bring them into it.

﴿O My servants, so fear Me﴾, and do not expose yourselves to what would incur My wrath. This is an admonition from Allah, the Exalted, that is far-reaching and encompasses the utmost of gentleness and mercy. It has been read as: ﴿O My servants﴾ (yā ʿibādī).

﴿And those who avoid the Taghut﴾. That is, the one who has reached the furthest extent of transgression. It is of the pattern فَعَلُوت (fa'lūt) derived from it, with the lām placed before the ʿayn. The pattern is built for intensifying the verbal noun, as in الرَّحَمُوت (ar-raḥamūt, "great mercy") and العَظَمُوت (al-ʿaẓamūt, "great majesty"). It was then used as a descriptive adjective for emphasis. The intended referent is Satan.

﴿that they worship it﴾ is a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal, a substitute whose meaning is included in the word it replaces) from it, since worshipping other than God Most High is worship of Satan, for it is he who commands it and makes it attractive.

﴿and turn in repentance to God﴾, and come to Him, turning away from all else with complete devotion.

﴿for them is good news﴾ of reward, conveyed through the tongues of the Messengers or the angels, at the time of the approach of death, when they are gathered, and after that.

﴿So give good tidings to My servants﴾

Those who listen to the word and follow the best of it: they are the ones described by *ijtinab* (avoidance of false deities and evil) and *inabah* (turning back to God in repentance) themselves. But the apparent noun was placed in the position of their pronoun, to honor them through the attribution and to indicate that the basis of their being characterized by these two noble qualities is that they are critics in religion, who distinguish truth from falsehood and prefer the best over the better.

﴿Those﴾ is a demonstrative pointing to them in view of their being characterized by the noble qualities mentioned. The sense of distance in it signals the loftiness of their rank and the remoteness of their station in excellence. Its position is nominative as the subject (*mubtada'*), and its predicate is what follows, the relative clause: those who are described by beautiful virtues.

﴿Those whom Allah has guided﴾ to the truth, ﴿and those are the people of understanding﴾: that is, they are the possessors of sound intellects, free from the opposition of illusion and the contention of desire, and they are the ones who deserve guidance and no others. In this is an indication that guidance is achieved through the act of God Most High and the soul's acceptance of it.

Abu al-Su'ud's commentary (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 39, verse 19:

﴿Is one against whom the word of punishment has been decreed [equal to one who is saved]? Can you, then, rescue whoever is in the Fire?﴾ This is a summary statement of the conditions opposite to those already mentioned, and a declaration that these people are deprived of guidance. They are the worshippers of the Taghut (every object of worship besides God) and those who follow its footsteps. This is hinted at by describing them as "those against whom the word of punishment has been decreed." What is meant by that word is God's saying to Iblis: ﴿I will surely fill Hell with you and with those among them who follow you, all together﴾, and His saying: ﴿Whoever follows you among them, I will surely fill Hell with all of you﴾.

The original form of the sentence is: "Is the one against whom the word of punishment has been decreed [such that] you rescue him?" It is a conditional sentence (شرطية, conditional), into which the interrogative hamzah (الهمزة, the interrogative particle) has entered to deny its content. Then the fa' (الفاء, the conjunctive particle fa) links it to a sentence that follows from it, which is implied after the hamzah, so that the denial and negation apply to both of its parts together. That is: "Are you the master of the affairs of people, so that whoever the word of punishment has been decreed against, you rescue him?" Then the hamzah is repeated in the apodosis (الجزاء) to emphasise the denial and to remind of it, since the speech has grown long. Then "whoever is in the Fire" (مَن في النّارِ) is placed in the position of a pronoun, to intensify the denial and the sense of its unlikelihood, and to draw attention to the fact that the one judged to receive punishment is in the status of one who has already entered the Fire. The Prophet's (ﷺ) efforts in calling them to faith are likewise a striving to save them from the Fire. It is also permissible for the apodosis to be omitted.

God's saying: "Can you, then...? etc." is an independent sentence, brought to confirm the content of the preceding sentence, to specify what was omitted from it, and to intensify the denial by treating the one who deserves punishment as one who has entered the Fire, and by depicting the effort in calling him to faith as the form of rescuing him from the Fire. It is as if it were said first: "Is the one against whom punishment has been decreed [such that] you deliver him from it?" Then the denial was intensified, and it was said: "Can you rescue whoever is in the Fire?" In this there is a hint that it is God alone who is able to rescue, and not anyone else. Since what is meant by "whoever is in the Fire" is those of whom it was said: ﴿For them there will be layers of Fire above them, and layers beneath them﴾, he made an exception from them with His saying:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 39, verse 20:

﴿But for those who have feared their Lord, there are chambers, above them chambers built up⁠﴾ And they are the ones who were addressed by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O My servants, so fear Me⁠﴾ and who were described by what was enumerated of the virtuous attributes. They are also the ones addressed earlier by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O My servants who have believed, fear your Lord⁠﴾ . . . the verse. He made clear that for them there are lofty ranks in the Gardens of Bliss, in contrast to the lowly degrees in the Fire that belong to the disbelievers; that is, for them are lofty chambers, some above others, ﴿built up⁠﴾ like the built dwellings founded upon the earth in solidity and firmness.

﴿Beneath them rivers flow⁠﴾ from beneath those chambers, ﴿the rivers⁠﴾, without any difference between the upper and the lower. ﴿The promise of Allah⁠﴾ is an emphatic infinitive (maṣdar mu'akkid) for His saying, exalted is He: "for them are chambers" . . . etc. For it is a promise, and what a promise!

﴿Allah does not fail in the promise⁠﴾, because failing in it is impossible for Him, glorified is He.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 39, verse 21:

﴿Have you not seen that Allah sends down water from the sky﴾ This is a resumptive sentence (istinaf), which comes either to give an analogy (tamthil) for the life of this world in its rapid passing and near vanishing, through what has been mentioned of the states of crops, as encouragement to turn away from its adornments and finery and as a warning against being deceived by its splendor, as in the parallels to His saying, ﴿The likeness of the life of this world is only like water﴾ . . . the verse. Or it comes to cite as evidence the certainty of what was promised concerning the rivers flowing beneath the lofty chambers, by what is witnessed of the sending down of water from the sky and what follows from it of the effects of His power, the perfection of His wisdom and His mercy. "Water" here means rain. It was also said that all water on earth comes from the sky, descending from it to the rock, and then Allah distributes it among the regions.

﴿Then He threads it﴾ that is, He makes it enter and arranges it ﴿into springs in the earth﴾ that is, channels and courses like the veins in bodies. It was also said that it means flowing waters in it, since the word yanbu' (spring) is applied both to the source and to what flows from it. Accordingly, "springs" is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal) on this second reading, and on the first reading the preposition is omitted, meaning "in springs."

﴿Then He brings forth thereby crops of varying colors﴾ that is, their kinds, such as wheat, barley and others; or their qualities, in colors, flavors and other respects. The word "then" (thumma) indicates sequence in rank or in time. The present tense is used to bring the scene vividly before the mind. ﴿Then it dries up﴾ that is, it completes its drying and approaches the point of being scattered from its roots.

﴿So you see it turn yellow﴾ after its greenness and freshness. It is also read as (mus-farrā'). ﴿Then He makes it into debris﴾ crushed, broken fragments, as though it had not flourished the day before. Because this state is among the strongly evident effects, it is attributed to Allah's making, just as the bringing forth is.

﴿Surely in that﴾ refers to what has been mentioned in detail, and the sense of distance in the demonstrative indicates the great remoteness of its status in strangeness and its pointing to what was intended to be explained.

﴿Is a reminder﴾ a great reminder ﴿for people of understanding﴾ for those whose intellects are pure of the flaws of defect, and an alert for them to the reality of the matter, so that they recall that the state of the life of this world, in its swift passing and cessation, is as they witness in the state of debris every year. Thus they are not deceived by its splendor nor tempted by its allurement. Or they are certain that He who is able to send down water from the sky and cause it to flow into the springs of the earth is able to cause rivers to flow beneath the chambers. This is the explanation. As for what has been said, that in this there is a reminder and an alert that there must be a wise Maker, and that this world exists by design and management, not by neglect and abandonment, that is far removed from the interpretation of this noble verse. Such a point would only suit a case where these noble effects and beautiful deeds were mentioned without being ascribed to any agent. Since they are here ascribed to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, it becomes clear that the object of the reminder and alert is His affairs, or the affairs of His effects, as has been explained, not His very existence, exalted is He. And the words of Allah, exalted is He:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 39, verse 22:

﴿Is one whose breast Allah has expanded for Islam...﴾ . . . etc. This is a resumptive clause functioning as a justification (ta'lil) for what precedes it, namely the restriction of the reminder to those endowed with understanding (ulu al-albab). The expansion of the breast for Islam (sharh al-sadr li'l-Islam) is an expression for the perfecting of the readiness for it, for it is the locus of the heart, which is the source of the spirit (ruh) to which the soul (nafs) that is receptive to Islam is attached. Thus its expansion requires the widening of the heart and its being illuminated by its light. It has been related that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When light enters the heart, it expands and opens." He was asked: "What is the sign of that?" He (ﷺ) said: "Turning in repentance (inabah) to the abode of eternity (dar al-khuld), withdrawing from the abode of delusion (dar al-ghurur), and preparing for death before its arrival." The discussion regarding the interrogative particle (hamza) and the fa' is like that which has passed concerning His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Is one upon whom the word of punishment has been justified...﴾. The predicate of "man" (man) is omitted, its indication being what follows it. The estimated meaning is: "Are all people equal? So whoever Allah has expanded his breast," that is, created him with an expanded breast, prepared for Islam, so he remained upon the original natural disposition (fitrah asliyyah), and it was not altered by acquired accidents that impair it.

﴿So he﴾, by virtue of that, is established ﴿upon light﴾ — a great light — ﴿from his Lord﴾, which is the divine grace (lutf ilahi) overflowing upon him at the witnessing of the cosmic signs (ayat takwiniyyah) and the revealed signs (ayat tanziliyyah), and the success (tawfiq) in being guided by them to the truth, unlike one whose heart has hardened and whose breast has become constricted, due to the alteration of the disposition of Allah through evil choice, and the darkness of error and misguidance has taken hold of him, so he turned away from those signs entirely, so that he neither remembers by them nor seizes them.

﴿So woe to those whose hearts are hardened against the remembrance of Allah﴾, that is, because of His remembrance, which by right should expand breasts and tranquilize hearts; that is, when Allah the Exalted is mentioned in their presence, or His signs, they recoil because of it, and their hearts grow harder, like His statement, exalted is He: ﴿so it increased them in uncleanness﴾. It has been read: (ʿan dhikr Allah), meaning: "from accepting it."

﴿Those﴾ are the remote ones described with what has been mentioned of hardness of hearts.

﴿In manifest error﴾ — far from the truth — ﴿clear﴾, its being error being evident to everyone. It was said that the verse was revealed concerning Hamzah and Ali, may Allah be pleased with them both, and Abu Lahab and his son; and it was said: concerning Ammar ibn (p-251) Yasir, may Allah be pleased with him, and Abu Jahl and his kin.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 39, verse 23:

﴿Allah has sent down the best of discourse﴾: this is the Noble Qur'an. It is related that the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) grew weary with a weariness, and they said to him (ﷺ): "Relate to us a narrative." And from Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them, they said: "If only you would relate to us." So this was revealed. The meaning is that in it there is a sufficiency (mandukha) from all other narratives. And in placing the Majestic Name at the beginning (as the subject) and in the construction of "nazzala" upon it, there is a magnification of "the best of discourse," an elevation of its station, a testimony to its excellence, an emphasis on its being ascribed to Him, the Exalted, and that it proceeds from Him and cannot proceed from another, and an alert that it is inimitable revelation, which is not hidden.

﴿Kitaban﴾ (a Book) is either a substitute (badal) for "the best of discourse," or a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of it, whether it has acquired definiteness from its genitive complement or not. For the occurrence of a circumstantial qualifier from an indefinite noun in construct is a matter of general permissibility, and its occurring as a circumstantial qualifier while being a noun rather than an adjective is either due to its being described by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿mutashabihan﴾ (similar in its parts), or because it is in the sense of "written" (maktuban). The meaning of its being "similar" is the similarity of its meanings in soundness, firmness, being founded upon truth and sincerity, entailing the benefits of creation in the Hereafter and in worldly life, the harmony of its words in eloquence, and the correspondence of its arrangement in inimitability.

﴿Mathani﴾ (oft-repeated) is another adjective of "Kitaban," or another circumstantial qualifier of it. It is the plural of "mathna," in the sense of what is repeated and reiterated, for what is recounted of its stories, reports, rulings, commands, prohibitions, promises, threats, and admonitions. It is said: because it is recited again and again in recitation. It is also said: it is the plural of "mafal" from "al-tathniya" in the sense of repetition and reiteration, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then return the gaze twice (kartayn)﴾, meaning, one return after another. Its occurring as an adjective of "Kitaban" is in consideration of its particulars, as one says "the Qur'an consists of suras and verses." It is also permissible that it be in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz) of "mutashabihan," as one says: "I saw a man good in his characteristics (shama'il)," meaning, "his characteristics." The meaning is: its oft-repeated parts are similar.

﴿The skins of those who fear their Lord shiver at it﴾: it is said to be an adjective of "Kitaban," or a circumstantial qualifier of it, since it is specified by the description. The more apparent view is that it is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) brought to explain its visible effects upon its hearers after explaining its attributes in itself, and to confirm that it is the best of discourse. "Iqshi'rar" means contraction. One says: "the skin shivered (iqsha'arra al-jild)" when it contracts with intense contraction, and its root is from "qash'" which is the dried hide, to which a "ra'" has been added so that it becomes quadriliteral and indicates an additional meaning. One says: "his skin shivered, his hair stood up," when intense fear befalls him from a fearsome reprehensible matter that overwhelms him suddenly. What is intended is either the explanation of the extremity of their fear by way of depiction and portrayal, or the explanation of the occurrence of that state and its befalling them by way of actual realization. The meaning is that when they hear the Qur'an and its striking verses of threat, awe and fear befall them, so that their skins shiver from them; and when they mention the mercy of Allah, Exalted is He, their fear is transformed into hope, and their dread into desire. This is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then their skins and their hearts soften to the remembrance of Allah﴾, meaning, tranquil and at rest in the remembrance of His mercy, Exalted is He. And the fact that it is not stated explicitly is an indication that it is the first thing that comes to mind upon the mention of Him, Exalted is He.

﴿That﴾, i.e., the Book whose states have been explained.

﴿The guidance of Allah; He guides by it whom He wills﴾: that He guides him by directing his capacity to being guided through contemplating what it contains of evidences of its truth and indications that it is from Allah, Exalted is He.

﴿And whomever Allah leaves astray﴾, i.e., He creates misguidance in him by directing His power toward its beginnings, and his turning away entirely from what would guide him to the truth, and his not being affected by its threat and promise at all; or (p-252) ﴿and whomever He forsakes﴾.

﴿Then he has no guide﴾ who would rescue him from the pit of misguidance. It is also said: that which has been mentioned of fear and hope is an effect of His guidance, Exalted is He; by that effect He guides whomever He wills of His servants; and "whomever He leaves astray," i.e., whom His kindness has not affected because of the hardness of his heart and his persistence in his sinfulness, then "he has no guide," i.e., no one who could have any influence upon him whatsoever.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 39, verse 24:

﴿Is one who shields with his face﴾ . . . etc. This is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) functioning as a justification (ta'lil) for what precedes it, namely the contrast between the states of the guided and the misguided. The discussion regarding the interrogative hamzah (alif of interrogation) and the fa' (fa' of consequence) and the omission of the predicate (khabar) is like that which has passed concerning its counterparts. The implied sense is: "Are all people equal? Rather, one whose condition is that he shields his self with his face, which is the most noble of his limbs."

﴿evil of the punishment﴾, i.e., the punishment that is evil and severe.

﴿on the Day of Resurrection﴾. Because his hand, with which he used to protect himself from hardships and dangers, is shackled to his neck, like one who is secure, to whom no harm befalls and who has no need to guard himself in any way. It is also said: it was revealed concerning Abu Jahl.

﴿And it will be said to the wrongdoers﴾ is coordinated (atf) upon "yattaqi" (shields), meaning: and it will be said to them by the keepers of the Fire. The past tense form is used to indicate certainty and establishment. It is also said that it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "yattaqi," with "qad" implied. Placing the explicit noun in the position of the pronoun serves to record their wrongdoing against them and to indicate the reason for the command in the words of the Exalted: ﴿Taste what you used to earn﴾, i.e., the consequence of what you used to earn in the world continuously, of disbelief and sins.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 39, verse 25:

﴿Those before them denied,﴾ a resumptive clause (isti'naf) brought to explain what punishment in this world befell some of the disbelievers, following the explanation of the punishment in the Hereafter that befalls all of them. That is: those before them among the earlier nations denied.

﴿Then the punishment came upon them﴾ that was decreed for each nation among them ﴿from where they did not perceive﴾ from the direction they did not reckon, and it did not occur to them that evil would come from it.

Abu al-Su'ud, Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim, on Surah 39 (al-Zumar), verse 26:

﴿So Allah made them taste disgrace﴾ That is: humiliation and abasement.

﴿in the life of this world﴾ such as transformation into animals, being swallowed up by the earth, killing, captivity, expulsion, and other kinds of punishment.

﴿And the punishment of the Hereafter﴾ prepared for them ﴿is greater﴾ because of its severity and its everlastingness ﴿if only they knew.﴾ That is: if it were within their capacity to know anything, they would have known that and taken warning from it.

And indeed We have set forth for mankind in this Qur'an every kind of parable, (parable: mathal, an illustrative example) which the one who reflects on the matters of his religion stands in need of.

﴿So that they may remember﴾: so that they may be mindful through it and take heed.

Qur'an in Arabic [as] a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) that is emphatic (muʾakkida) of "this" (min hādhā); the basis of the emphasis is the descriptive quality, as in your saying: "Zayd came to me, a righteous man," or it is praise of it.

Free of any crookedness (ghayr dhī ʿiwaj): there is no discrepancy in it in any respect whatsoever. It is more eloquent than "straight" (mustaqīm) and more specific in its meanings. It has also been said that what is meant by "crookedness" (ʿiwaj) is doubt.

So that they may be mindful (laʿallahum yattaqūn): a second cause (ʿilla), consequent upon the first.

God presents an example: a man in whom are partners at odds with one another (﴿ضَرَبَ اللَّهُ مَثَلا رَجُلا فِيهِ شُرَكاءُ مُتَشاكِسُونَ﴾)

This is one of the Qur'anic parables (amthal). After stating that the purpose of presenting them is remembrance, taking admonition from them, and attaining taqwa (God-consciousness), the author explains that the meaning of "ḍaraba al-mathal" (to present a parable) here is to apply a strange situation to another similar one and make it like it, as was discussed in the commentary on Surah Yasin. The word "mathalan" is the second object of "ḍaraba," and "rajulan" is its first object. The first object has been placed after the second to create suspense about it, and so that what completes it, which is the essential part of the illustration, may be joined to it. The phrase "fīhi" is not a relative clause (ṣilah) modifying "shurakā'," as some have said. Rather, it is the predicate (khabar) of "shurakā'," and explaining that it was originally so is unnecessary. The clause is in the accusative position as a description of "rajulan," or the description is the prepositional phrase "fīhi," and "shurakā'" is raised by it as the subject, because it depends on the noun it describes. The meaning is that God has made a parable for the polytheist, according to what his creed leads to: the claim that each of his deities has a claim to his servitude, so that he becomes a slave shared by a group who pull at him and take turns with him in their different affairs, so that he is bewildered and his heart is divided.

﴿وَرَجُلا﴾ (and a man): that is, a man was made a parable for the monotheist.

﴿سَلَمًا﴾ (wholly): that is, purely belonging ﴿لِرَجُلٍ﴾ (to one man), a single person over whom no one else has any claim at all. It is also read as "salman" with a fatḥah and with a kasrah on the sin, with the lam sukūn, and all of these are verbal nouns (maṣādir) from "salima lahu kadhā," meaning "it became pure for him." It is used as a qualifier for intensification (mubālaghah), or the word dhū (possessor) has been omitted from it. It is also read as "sālimān" and "sālimun," meaning: and there is a man who is sound (sālim).

The singling out of the man is because he is more aware of what befalls him of harm and benefit.

﴿هَلْ يَسْتَوِيانِ مَثَلا﴾ (Are the two equal in description?): this is a denial and a declaration of improbability of their being equal, and a negation of that in the most eloquent and emphatic manner, and a notice that this is so clear and evident that no one can utter that they are equal, or hesitate in judging that they differ, since one of them is in the highest of the highest heavens and the other is in the lowest of the lowest. This is the secret behind leaving the superior and the inferior unspecified, and the accusative of "mathalan" as a specification (tamyīz). That is: Are their two conditions and their two descriptions equal? Limiting the specification to the singular is to show the category. It is also read as "mathalayni" (two examples), like His saying, ﴿أكْثَرُ أمْوالا وأوْلادًا﴾ (more in wealth and children), with a difference of type; or because the intended meaning is whether the two are equal in the two descriptions, with the pronoun referring to the two examples, since the estimate is "the example of a man in whom..." and "the example of a man..."

His saying, ﴿الحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ﴾ (Praise be to God), is a confirmation of what precedes it, namely the negation of equality, by way of parenthetical insertion (i'tirāḍ), and an alert to the monotheists that the excellence they possess is by God's grace, and that this is a great blessing that obliges them to persist in praising Him and worshipping Him. Or it is on the basis that His explaining through the presenting of parables that they have the highest example, and that the polytheists have the example of evil, is a beautiful act and a complete kindness from Him, glorious and majestic, which deserves His praise and worship.

His saying, ﴿بَلْ أكْثَرُهم لا يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ (But most of them do not know), is a turning away (iḍrāb) and a transition from explaining the non-equality in the aforementioned manner to explaining that most people, namely the polytheists, do not know this even though it is perfectly evident, so they remain in the predicament of polytheism and error.

His saying, the Exalted:

Qur'anic quotation: ﴿Indeed, you will die, and indeed they will die.﴾ This is a preface (tamhid) to what follows of disputing on the Day of Resurrection. It is also recited as (ماﺉِتٌ) and (ماﺉِتُونَ) [mā'itun and mā'itūn], i.e., "dying" in the active participle form. It was said: they were waiting for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to die, meaning: all of you are on the verge of death.

Then indeed you, on the Day of Resurrection, before your Lord (i.e., the Master of your affairs) will be disputing (﴿تَخْتَصِمُونَ﴾). So you will argue against them, saying that you conveyed to them what you were sent with of rulings and admonitions, among which are those contained within the verses of this passage, and that you strove in calling to the truth with the utmost striving, while they persisted in obstinacy and stubbornness. It has also been said that what is meant by it is the general dispute that takes place in this world among mankind. The first is the more apparent and more suitable in view of His saying (p-254) the Exalted:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 39, verse 32:

﴿Who then is more unjust than he who lies against Allah﴾. Then, "it" (i.e., the verse) through to its end is brought (lit. "driven," maswuq) solely to explain the condition of each of the two parties to the dispute (al-ikhtisam, the contention) that is ongoing concerning disbelief and belief. That is: more unjust than every wrongdoer is the one who fabricates against Allah, glorified and exalted is He, by ascribing to Him a partner and a son.

﴿And denies the truth﴾: that is, the matter which is the very essence of the truth and the very reality of truthfulness, namely what the Prophet (ﷺ) brought.

﴿When it comes to him﴾: that is, at the very first time it comes to him, without reflection upon it or consideration of it.

﴿Is there not in Hell an abode for the disbelievers?﴾: that is, for those who fabricated against Allah, glorified is He, and hastened to deny the truth from the very beginning. The plural is used in view of the meaning of "man" (man), just as the singular is used in the preceding pronouns in view of its wording. Or it refers to the category of disbelievers, and they are included in the ruling by primary inclusion (dukhulan awwaliyyan).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 39, verse 33:

﴿And he who brings the truth and confirms it﴾. The relative pronoun (al-mawsul) refers to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and those who follow him, just as the referent in His statement, ﴿And We indeed gave Musa the Book, that they might be guided﴾, is Musa, peace be upon him, and his people. It has also been said that it refers to the generic class of messengers and the believers in them. This is supported by the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him: "Those who brought the truth and confirmed it" (وَالَّذِينَ جَاءُوا بِالصِّدْقِ وَصَدَّقُوا بِهِ). It has also been said that it is an attributive clause modifying an omitted noun, namely "the group" (al-fawj) or "the party" (al-fariq).

﴿Those﴾: those described by what has been mentioned, namely bringing the truth and confirming it.

﴿They are the God-fearing﴾: those characterized by taqwa (God-consciousness), which is the most noble of desirable qualities. It was also read as "wa-sadaqa bihi" (وَصَدَقَ بِهِ) with light pronunciation, meaning that he conveyed it to the people and delivered it to them as it was revealed to him, without alteration. It has also been said that it means he became truthful through it, i.e., because of it, since the Qur'an that he brought is a miracle indicating his truthfulness (ﷺ). It was also read as "ṣuddiqa bihi" (صُدِّقَ بِهِ) in the passive voice.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 39, verse 34:

﴿For them is whatever they wish with their Lord﴾ is an explanation of what they have in the Hereafter of good outcome (husn al-ma'ab), after the explanation of what they have in this world of excellent deeds (mahasin al-a'mal). That is: for them is everything they wish of bringing benefits and warding off harms in the Hereafter, not in Paradise alone, because some of what they wish for, namely the expiation of misdeeds and security from the Greatest Terror (al-faza' al-akbar) and the rest of the horrors of the Resurrection, occurs only before entry into Paradise.

﴿That﴾ refers to what has been mentioned of the attainment of everything they wish for.

﴿is the recompense of the good-doers (al-muhsinin)﴾: that is, those who made their deeds good (ahsanu a'malahum). The meaning of ihsan (excellence) has been explained more than once before. And His, exalted is He, saying:

﴿So that God may expiate from them the worst of what they did﴾ ... etc. This is connected to His words, exalted is He, ﴿They will have whatever they wish﴾, but not in terms of its explicit wording, since it is inconceivable that the aforementioned expiation be the purpose of their being granted whatever they wish in the Hereafter. How could it be otherwise, when it is part of what will be granted to them there? Rather, it is connected in terms of its implied meaning (fahwa). Since it is not a report of what was granted to them in the past, but of what will be granted to them in the future, it has the sense of a promise of it, as mentioned in His words, exalted is He, ﴿the promise of God﴾, for it is an emphatic infinitive (masdar mu'akkid) for what precedes it, His words, exalted is He, ﴿For them are chambers, above which are chambers built﴾, since its meaning is "God promised them chambers." Thus "the promise of God" is in the accusative governed by it, as if it were said: God promised them everything they wish for, namely the removal of harms and the attainment of joys, so that He may expiate for them, in accordance with that promise, the worst of what they did, to repel their harms.

﴿And He will reward them with the best of what they used to do﴾, granting them their benefits. The use of the noble Name (Allah) in the place of a pronoun serves to show the full concern with the content of the statement. The annexation of "the worst" (al-aswa') and "the best" (al-ahsan) to what follows them is not of the type of annexation of the superior to the thing it surpasses (idafat al-mufaddal ila al-mufaddal 'alayhi, i.e., the comparative construction), but of the annexation of a thing to a part of itself, intended for emphasis and clarification, without considering its preference over it. What is considered in both is mere excellence and increase, not over a specific, particular annexed noun, as in the saying: "Al-Naqis and al-Ashajj were the two most just of the Banu Marwan." Except that the increase considered in them is not in the strict literal sense. Rather, in the first, it is with regard to what befits their condition, namely magnifying their evil deeds however small, and belittling their good deeds however great. In the second, it is with regard to the kindness of the Most Generous of the generous, in regarding a small good deed as great and matching it with abundant rewards. Taking the increase literally is possible in the first case as well. This is based on the premise that singling out "the worst" for mention is to indicate that what is less than it is expiated by way of priority (al-awla), since expiating the worst necessarily entails expiating the lesser evil. But since this does not apply to "the best," it was best to arrange both in one line with respect to the consideration. The combining of the two forms, the past and the future, in the relative clause of the second relative pronoun, but not the first, is to indicate the continuance of their performing righteous deeds, unlike the evil deed.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 39, verse 36:

﴿Is not Allah sufficient for His servant?﴾ This is a denial and negation of His not being sufficient, in the most emphatic and forceful form, as if sufficiency is so established and evident that no one could dare to utter its absence, or would stammer in answering with its existence. By "the servant" ('abd) is meant either the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or the category (jins) that includes him, peace be upon him, in a primary sense of inclusion. This is supported by the reading of one who reads ( 'ibadahu ) (His servants), which is interpreted as "the Prophets," peace be upon them. Likewise is the reading of one who reads ( bi-kafi 'ibadihi ) with the genitive construction. The form ( yukafi'u 'abadahu ) is the form of mughalaba (contest, i.e., a form expressing one party striving to overcome another), either from kifaya (sufficiency), to convey intensification of it, or from mukafa'a (requital) in the sense of recompense. This is a consolation to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) regarding what the Quraysh said to him: "We fear that our gods will afflict you with madness, and that harm from them will befall you because of your reviling them." In another narration they said: "You shall surely desist from reviling our gods, or some insanity or madness from them will surely strike you." Just as the people of Hud said: ﴿We say nothing except that some of our gods have struck you with evil﴾ (Hud 11:54). This is His statement, exalted is He: ﴿and they frighten you with those besides Him﴾, that is, the idols which they took as gods besides Allah, exalted is He. The clause is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf, a new independent sentence), and it has been said that it is a circumstantial clause (hal, a clause describing the state of the subject).

﴿And whoever Allah leaves astray﴾ so that he becomes heedless of His sufficiency, of His protection of him (ﷺ), and of His ability to bring benefit and harm at all.

﴿then there is no guide for him﴾ who would guide him to any good whatsoever.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 39, verse 37:

﴿And whomever Allah guides, there is no misleader for him.﴾ He diverts him from his purpose, or afflicts him with harm that disrupts his conduct, since none can repel His act or oppose His will, as His saying the Exalted indicates: ﴿Is not Allah Mighty﴾, Victorious who cannot be overcome, Invincible who cannot be resisted or contended with.

﴿Lord of retribution﴾, who takes vengeance on His enemies on behalf of His friends. The placing of the glorious Name (al-ism al-jalil) in the position of the pronoun (al-idmar) is to affirm the content of the statement and to instill awe.

(p-256) ﴿And if you ask them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?" they will surely say, "Allah."﴾ This is because the proof is clear and the way is plain.

﴿Say﴾ (to rebuke them): ﴿Have you considered what you invoke besides Allah? If Allah should intend for me some harm, would they be removers of His harm? Or if He should intend for me some mercy, would they be withholders of His mercy?﴾ That is: after you have become certain that the Creator of the upper and lower worlds is Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, tell me: if Allah intends for me some harm, would your gods remove that harm from me?

﴿Or if He intends for me mercy﴾, that is: or if He intends for me some benefit.

﴿Would they be withholders of His mercy﴾, so as to withhold it from me? It is also recited as "kāshifātun ḍurrihi" and "mumsikātun raḥmatahu" with tanwin in both, with ḍurrahu and raḥmatahu in the accusative. The conditional clause concerning the intention of harm or mercy is attached to Allah Himself (ﷺ, peace and blessings be upon him) in order to refute them to their faces, since they had threatened him with the harm of the idols, and because it conveys sincere counsel in its purest form.

﴿Say: Allah is sufficient for me﴾, that is, in all my affairs, in attaining good and warding off evil. It is narrated that when the Prophet (ﷺ) asked them, they fell silent, and then this was revealed: ﴿In Him put their trust those who trust﴾, not in anything else at all, because they know that everything other than Him lies under His dominion, exalted is He.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 39, verse 39:

﴿Say: "O my people, act according to your position (ʿalā makānatikum)"﴾ — that is, according to your state in which you are, of the enmity in which you have become firmly established. The word makāna (position, station) is borrowed from the noun ʿayn (place, i.e., a concrete location) for the meaning, as it is borrowed here, and ḥayth (where) is used for time although both are for place. It is also read: ʿalā makānātikum (in the plural). ﴿Indi ʿāmilun﴾ — that is, "according to my position." It has been omitted for brevity, for emphasis in the threat, and to indicate that his state continues to grow in strength through the help and support of God, Mighty and Majestic. For this reason He threatened them with his being victorious over them in both abodes, by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So you will soon know﴾.

Whoever will be visited by a punishment that disgraces him (﴿مَن يَأْتِيهِ عَذابٌ يُخْزِيهِ﴾). The disgrace of his enemies is a proof of his (peace and blessings be upon him) victory over them, and Allah the Exalted punished them and disgraced them on the Day of Badr.

﴿وَيَحِلُّ عَلَيْهِ عَذابٌ مُقِيمٌ﴾ That is: the punishment that lasts, which is the punishment of the Fire, is everlasting.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 39, verse 41:

﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you the Book for mankind﴾ — for their sake, for it is the basis of their welfare in this life and the Hereafter.

﴿With truth﴾ — a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) referring either to the subject of "sent down" (i.e., We) or to its object (i.e., the Book).

﴿So whoever is guided﴾ — by acting upon what is in it.

﴿it is for his own self﴾ — that is, he benefits only his own self thereby.

﴿And whoever goes astray﴾ — by not acting in accordance with its requirements.

﴿then he strays only to his own detriment﴾ — because the harm of his straying is confined to himself.

﴿And you are not a guardian over them﴾ — so that you could compel them to guidance. Your duty is only to convey the message, and you have indeed conveyed it in the fullest manner.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 39, verse 42:
